evidence.title: SoftBank's Great Indian Exit: What the Meesho, Lenskart, and Ola Electric Sales Really Mean
evidence.text:
SoftBank is having a garage sale in India, and everyone's watching. The Japanese investment giant has been systematically trimming its stakes in some of the country's most celebrated startups—Meesho, Lenskart Solutions, and Ola Electric Mobility. In just a few months, these sales have piled up to over ₹11,000 crore. But this isn't a panic sell. It's a calculated, methodical monetisation of investments that have delivered handsome returns. The story here isn't about SoftBank losing faith in India. It's about a global investment powerhouse recycling capital, managing its massive AI bets, and responding to a market that's finally rewarding fundamentals over hype.
Let's look at the numbers. In November 2026 alone, SoftBank sold a 1.65% stake in Meesho for ₹1,885 crore through a block deal on the National Stock Exchange. This followed a 1.7% sale in September for ₹1,650 crore. That's roughly ₹3,535 crore realised from Meesho in two tranches. The pattern is similar at Lenskart. SoftBank offloaded stakes worth ₹2,873 crore in June, ₹2,888 crore in August, and another ₹1,896 crore in November 2026. That's about ₹7,657 crore from Lenskart alone. Add it all up, and SoftBank has pulled out approximately ₹11,192 crore (around $1.2–1.3 billion) from these two winners in just a few months.
Between January and October 2026, it sold about 1.2 percentage points of its stake, leaving it with roughly 11.7%. The reason is simple: Ola Electric's stock has plummeted about 54% from its listing price, and the company is still loss-making. SoftBank's own valuation shows its Ola investment is worth about 30% less than what it put in. You sell your winners, not your losers. That's portfolio management 101. Other
SoftBank hasn't publicly explained its reasoning, but the data points to several clear drivers. First, lock-in periods have expired. Lenskart's lock-in ended in May 2026, and Meesho's likely lapsed by mid-2026 since it listed in December 2025. This is the natural window for early investors to cash out. Second, the stocks are trading near all-time highs. Meesho is up about 58% from its listing-day open, and Lenskart has soared 84%. Selling into strength makes sense when you've made a killing.
Third, and perhaps most importantly, SoftBank needs capital for its global AI ambitions. The group has poured a staggering $64.6 billion into OpenAI, including a $30 billion follow-on investment completed in three tranches through October 2026. It's also planning a €75 billion investment in AI data centers in Europe. The Indian proceeds, while significant, are small change against these numbers. They represent about 4% of the OpenAI follow-on and roughly 6% of SoftBank's public investment portfolio. But every bit helps when you're making bets of this magnitude.
The returns on these investments are extraordinary. SoftBank's Vision Fund 2 invested about $225 million in Lenskart and $285 million in Meesho. By September 2026, the gross returns on these investments had swelled to $1.3 billion and $642 million respectively. That's a roughly 5.8x multiple on Lenskart and 2.3x on Meesho. The recent sales have converted some of those paper gains into cold, hard cash.
For Lenskart, SoftBank's weighted average acquisition cost was about ₹74.26 per share. The three block sales happened at prices ranging from roughly ₹508 to ₹697. On the shares sold, SoftBank realised about 8 times its cost. For Meesho, the exact cost isn't public, but the ₹3,535 crore in proceeds likely represents about 1.3–1.5 times the capital invested. SoftBank has already recovered its full Lenskart investment and more. For Meesho, it's well on its way. DRHP
Here's the fascinating part: as SoftBank exits, a new class of investors is stepping in. The Meesho block deal attracted 16 domestic and foreign institutional investors. Fidelity Investments emerged as the largest buyer, picking up about 2.32 crore shares worth ₹573 crore across eight schemes. Societe Generale bought 1.47 crore shares for ₹365 crore, making it the largest single named buyer. Domestic mutual funds like Motilal Oswal, HDFC, Edelweiss, and Aditya Birla Sun Life also participated, alongside Bajaj Allianz Life Insurance.
Even sovereign wealth funds joined the party. The Government of Singapore, Monetary Authority of Singapore, and Norway's Government Pension Fund Global all acquired shares. This is significant. These are typically long-horizon, low-turnover holders. Their presence suggests confidence in Meesho's long-term prospects despite SoftBank's departure. It also points to a broader shift in ownership from early venture backers to institutional investors who demand quarterly results and clear paths to profitability.
SoftBank's sell-down is a signal, but not necessarily a negative one. It shows that public markets in India have matured enough to absorb large secondary sales without collapsing. Both Meesho and Lenskart shares actually closed higher on the days of their block deals. That's a vote of confidence in the companies' fundamentals.
However, the broader funding environment is becoming more selective. Late-stage funding in India fell 27% year-on-year in the first half of 2026 to $2.2 billion. Mega-rounds of $100 million or more are becoming rarer. Investors are increasingly focused on unit economics, capital efficiency, and credible paths to profitability. The era of growth at all costs is giving way to a more disciplined approach.
For Meesho specifically, the shift in ownership has implications. The company is still loss-making, though its losses are narrowing and its contribution margin has improved to 6% of net merchandise value from 3.3% a year earlier. Its cash balance of about ₹7,048 crore provides a substantial buffer. But with a more diversified institutional shareholder base, management will face greater scrutiny on spending and profitability. The pressure to deliver on margins will only increase. Investor Presentation
SoftBank's actions need to be viewed through the lens of its global strategy. The group is pivoting aggressively towards artificial intelligence. It liquidated its entire stake in Nvidia worth $5.8 billion to redirect capital towards OpenAI. The Indian stake sales are part of this broader recycling of capital. SoftBank is harvesting returns from mature investments in consumer internet and e-commerce to fuel its next big bet.
This doesn't mean SoftBank is done with India. The group remains a major foreign investor with nearly $16 billion deployed in Indian startups to date. But the nature of its involvement is changing. It's moving from being a long-term holder in growth-stage companies to a more active portfolio manager that monetises winners when valuations are rich.
For Meesho and Lenskart, the immediate challenge is to prove they can grow into their rich valuations. Meesho trades at roughly 7.9 times its trailing twelve-month sales, while Lenskart is at about 12.2 times. These are premium multiples that will be hard to sustain without consistent execution on profitability.
For SoftBank, the question is whether it will continue to trim its remaining stakes. It still holds about 5.19% of Meesho and roughly 5.7% of Lenskart. Further sales are likely if the stocks hold up. For Ola Electric, the path is murkier. Until the company demonstrates a turnaround, SoftBank is likely stuck with a position that's underwater.
For India's startup ecosystem, SoftBank's sell-down is a coming-of-age moment. It shows that public markets can provide meaningful exits for early investors. It also signals that the days of easy money are over. The next generation of startups will need to build enduring businesses with sustainable economics, not just chase unicorn status. The bar has been raised, and that's ultimately a good thing for the ecosystem's long-term health.

evidence.title: Ola Electric shares fall 6% after Q2 results: Goldman Sachs says 'SELL'! Why does it see 37% downside?
evidence.text:
Shares of Ola Electric Mobility declined on Friday, November 13, after the electric two-wheeler maker reported its September quarter results, with investors assessing the company's falling revenue, continued losses and challenges in its business transition.
Ola Electric shares fell as much as 6.32 per cent during the session to an intraday low of Rs 33.48, compared with the previous closing price of Rs 35.74. At around 10:31 am, the stock was trading at Rs 34.80, down Rs 0.94 or 2.63 per cent on the NSE.
The decline came even as the company's consolidated net loss narrowed on a year-on-year basis. However, a sharp fall in revenue and concerns over its dealer-led distribution strategy continued to weigh on the company's outlook.
Goldman Sachs has maintained its bearish stance on the stock and reduced its target price. Here is what investors need to know.
Ola Electric reported a consolidated net loss of Rs 362 crore for the July-September quarter of FY27, compared with a net loss of Rs 418 crore in the corresponding quarter of the previous financial year.
While the company's net loss narrowed by around 13.4 per cent year-on-year, its revenue from operations declined sharply.
Revenue fell nearly 39 per cent to Rs 421 crore in Q2 FY27 from Rs 690 crore in the year-ago period.
The company's total expenses also declined during the quarter. Expenses stood at Rs 639 crore, down 28 per cent from Rs 893 crore in the corresponding period last year.
The financial performance indicates that although Ola Electric has managed to reduce its losses and expenses, the decline in revenue remains a key concern.
Ola Electric's automotive segment reported a loss of Rs 214 crore in the September quarter, compared with Rs 233 crore in Q2 FY26.
However, revenue from the automotive segment declined to Rs 420 crore from Rs 688 crore in the year-ago quarter.
The company's cell segment also continued to report losses. The segment posted a net loss of Rs 84 crore in Q2 FY27, compared with Rs 79 crore in the corresponding quarter last year.
Revenue from the cell segment stood at Rs 3 crore against Rs 4 crore a year ago.
In its shareholder letter, Ola Electric said it had achieved the scheduled commercial operation date (SCOD) for 6 GWh of cell manufacturing capacity ahead of schedule.
The company is now ramping up production and improving yields. It also said the government had extended its Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme support until calendar year 2031.
Ola Electric expects PLI incentives to start coming in from the next quarter, as it is already ahead of its PLI milestones.
Another important development for Ola Electric is its ongoing restructuring of the retail distribution network.
The company is transitioning from company-owned stores to a dealer-led distribution model. It opened its first dealer store on September 4 and had expanded its network to 319 outlets by November 8.
The company aims to establish 700 outlets by the fourth quarter of FY27.
Ola Electric expects the transition to help reduce its operating expenses. In its shareholder letter, the company said operating expenses would further decline by around Rs 50 crore as it shuts down its company-owned store network.
However, the transition also comes with execution risks, particularly regarding the company's ability to maintain sales volumes and profitability through the dealer-led model.
Global brokerage Goldman Sachs maintained its 'Sell' rating on Ola Electric shares and reduced its target price to Rs 22 from Rs 23.
The brokerage highlighted risks associated with the company's transition to a dealer-led distribution model.
Goldman Sachs expects gross margin pressure of more than 650 basis points due to the distribution transition. However, it believes some of this pressure could be offset by fixed-cost savings of around Rs 500 million.
The brokerage also reduced its FY27-FY29 revenue estimates by up to 6 per cent, citing weak volumes and continued losses.
The reduction in the target price indicates that Goldman Sachs remains cautious about the company's near-term business prospects despite its efforts to reduce operating expenses.
Goldman Sachs' revised target price of Rs 22 suggests further downside for Ola Electric shares from their current market price. At Rs 34.80, the stock is trading around 58 per cent above the brokerage's revised target price.

From a market performance perspective, Ola Electric shares have delivered negative returns across several periods. The stock has declined 0.83 per cent over one month, 7.22 per cent year-to-date and 17.51 per cent over one year.
In comparison, the Nifty 500 has gained 7.85 per cent over one month and has declined just 0.36 per cent year-to-date. Over one year, the index has remained almost unchanged, with a marginal gain of 0.04 per cent.

evidence.title: Can Ola Electric’s pivot to dealership model hedge revenue decline?
evidence.text:
Ola Electric Mobility Ltd’s September quarter (Q2FY27) brought no relief, with the electric two-wheeler maker reporting a higher-than-expected consolidated Ebitda loss of ₹218 crore. The company’s revenue was down 39% year-on-year to ₹421 crore.
Ola’s revenue has shrunk from about ₹5,000 crore in FY24 to ₹2,250 crore in FY26. H1FY27 revenue declined 42% year-on-year to ₹875 crore. The revenue plunge reflects Ola’s move from a high-growth, company-owned, direct-to-consumer (D2C) model to a dealership-based model.
The transition is yet to translate into better quarterly operating performances. Ola needs this shift to yield the desired results in terms of recovering volumes and protecting profit margins.
India’s electric two-wheeler market is expanding rapidly, with industry volumes reaching 599,000 units in Q2, up almost 83% year-on-year, as per government vehicle registration data. But Ola’s growth trajectory has diverged. However, Ola’s vehicle deliveries were down 34% year-on-year to 34,667 units in Q2.
The trend persisted in October too, when electric two-wheeler registrations reached 224,064 units, up 48% year-on-year, while Ola’s dropped by 26% to about 12,000 units. Ola’s market share narrowed to 5.4% in October from about 35% in 2024.
“The company will have to sustainably reach 25,000 monthly volumes in order to achieve cash breakeven levels,” said analysts from Kotak Institutional Equities. They added that the quarterly consolidated free cash flow outflow of ₹350 crore remains an area of concern.
On the Q2 earnings call, Ola’s management said demand now exceeds supply, citing a paid-order backlog and delayed delivery of roughly 5,000 units due to a charger shortage.
Ola’s shift from company-owned stores to dealerships is progressing rapidly. The first dealer store was opened on 4 September, and by 8 November, the company had 255 dealers with 319 operational stores. It plans to expand to 450 stores by December and 700 by March.
Dealer commissions
The model can help reduce the fixed cost of operating front-end sales touchpoints, shift the inventory and part of the working capital burden to dealers and potentially improve sales and service reach. The management expects the current gross margin of 30% to be adversely affected in the near term due to dealer commissions.
Ola’s real advantage lies in vertical integration. Designing vehicles, in-house components and its own battery packs help it to reduce the bills-of-materials cost by 15% to 20% as compared to rivals, said the management.
Ola plans to ramp up its 6 GWh cell factory, integrate nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells into vehicles, launch its Shakti energy storage products and eventually expand cell capacity towards 20 GWh, subject to successful yield, demand and funding. The expansion of the dealer network and the cell plant is yet to show in the revenue numbers.
Ola’s shares traded more than 3% lower on Friday as investor hopes of a turnaround were dashed. The near-term outlook depends on whether the dealer-led transition converts into retail volumes and lower fixed costs, and the cell manufacturing and deeper vertical integration deliver on the promised cost benefits.
Ola needs to demonstrate sustained demand recovery. Until then, the stock is likely to remain sensitive to operational milestones and the management guidance.

evidence.title: SMM Net Zero Europe 2026: Navigating Europe’s Energy Transition, Opening a New Chapter for PV+ESS
evidence.text:
On November 3, the Net Zero Europe 2026 - Solar & Energy Storage Summit, organized by Shanghai Metals Market (SMM) and supported by Catalonia Trade & Investment (ACCIÓ) and the Government of Catalonia, Spain, concluded successfully at the Hilton Barcelona, Spain! This event is Europe's premier deal-focused leadership summit, bringing together senior decision-makers, project developers, utilities, investors, and technology innovators shaping the future of solar, energy storage, and grid flexibility.
During the keynote sessions, speakers shared insights on a lot of hot topics, including:
- From Reactive to Proactive: Maximising Asset Value Through Advanced O&M Strategies in Europe’s Solar-Storage Era
- From China to Europe: The Reshaping of the Photovoltaic Supply Chain and a New Chapter in the Industrial Landscape
- How CPV technology can shape the future of solar energy conversion
- Designing hybrid systems to generate long-term value
- Rethinking BESS for Evolving Grids: How String PCS and Grid-Forming Capability Deliver Long-Term Asset Value
- Machine Learning, AI agents and grid modelling to earn more with flexible assets
 
In addition, SMM organized multiple rounds of panel sessions, bringing together renowned enterprise leaders, scholars, and industry experts from leading enterprises to engage in insightful discussions on Europe's PV+ESS industry, including:
- From Gigawatt Ambition to Bankable Reality: The Rise of Europe's Massive Solar-Storage Hybrids
- Powering the AI Revolution: How Data Centres Become the Next Catalyst for Solar-Storage Growth in Europe
- How Leading PV & Energy Storage Enterprises Define PV-Storage Integration
- How Next-Generation Module Technologies (TOPCon, HJT, BC, CPV) Reshape Project Profitability in Europe
- A Key Pillar of European Energy Transition: Unlocking the Growth Potential of Distributed Solar-Storage
》Click here to view the photo gallery of the event
Opening Remarks
Adam Fan, Chairman of SMM
Keynote Speech: From Reactive to Proactive: Maximising Asset Value Through Advanced O&M Strategies in Europe’s Solar-Storage Era
Speaker: Jonás de Miguel, Senior Director Global O&M at Recurrent Energy
Panel Discussion: From Gigawatt Ambition to Bankable Reality: The Rise of Europe's Massive Solar-Storage Hybrids
Moderator: Lluís Millet Biosca, Head of Advisory at One Hub Energy
Panelists:
Jens Gobel, Co-Founder of AXO Energy
Alvaro Sanz, Global Head of Development at ENERSIDE ENERGY
Amber Wang, Vice President of Corporate Finance & Investments at Ampyr Solar Europe
Bhavuk Chugh, Director of Northern Europe at Centrica Energy Trading
Eric Wang, CEO of International Business at CRRC
The panelists discussed the PV+ESS landscape in Spain as an example, noting that Spain has accumulated over 1,000 hours of zero or negative electricity prices, with approximately 10 GW of PV assets facing debt repayment difficulties, which has created an urgent demand for energy storage solutions. At the same time, 34 GW of energy storage projects in Spain have obtained grid connection permits, but bankability remains the core bottleneck for project deployment. In Spain, the value premium from adding cells to existing PV assets ranges from 20,000 to 30,000 euros per megawatt, depending on grid feed-in and feed-out connection constraints as well as existing power purchase agreement (PPA) terms.
Partial toll processing covers 70%–80% of cell capacity, locking in most revenue to satisfy lenders while retaining some spot upside and avoiding penalty liquidated damages triggered by unavailable capacity. Meanwhile, lenders require 50%–60% of capacity to have 5–7 years of contracted revenue, which aligns with this structure. Competition then shifts to these more specific metrics: grid connection compliance, performance guarantees (availability, round-trip efficiency, usable energy), cybersecurity, carbon footprint, and long-term supplier viability.
Keynote Speech: The reality in BESS projects
Speaker: Michael Alexander Strobel, European Business Director, Great Power
Panel Discussion: Powering the AI Revolution: How Data Centres Become the Next Catalyst for Solar-Storage Growth in Europe
Panelists:
Salvador Salat, Delegate for Catalonia
Paolo Sammartino, Chief Operating Officer of Renexia
Keynote Speech:  From China to Europe: The Reshaping of the Photovoltaic Supply Chain and a New Chapter in the Industrial Landscape
Speaker: Uriel Wang, Senior Analyst for PV and Power Market, SMM
Uriel Wang stated that global new installations are expected to decline by around 23% YoY in 2026, followed by a recovery at a 9.0% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) through 2030. As Europe and the US slow down, emerging markets will contribute more growth; localization policies and trade barriers are reshaping the global manufacturing footprint, while China remains the primary export source and maintains its price and efficiency advantages in modules.
Global PV Installations: Growth Shifts to Emerging Markets
Global installations reset in 2026. Slowing growth in mature markets shifts incremental demand to emerging regions.
SMM expects global PV installations in 2026 to edge down YoY from 2025, though from 2026 to 2030, global PV installations will rise steadily, with an estimated CAGR of around 9%. Among these, Southeast Asia, as a representative emerging market, will significantly outperform the global average——Indonesia's proposed 100 GW PV installation target, its 45% renewable energy generation share target, and rapidly growing local electricity demand will together form the primary drivers of installation growth in the region.
Ex-China PV Market Weakens Amid Protectionism and Localization Expansion
Energy security, industrial policy, and geopolitics are driving measures to reduce reliance on Chinese PV products and prioritize domestic manufacturing, directly impacting Chinese PV exports.
Panel Discussion:How Leading PV & Energy Storage Enterprises Define PV-Storage Integration
Moderator: Jingyi Chen, Co-founder and CEO of Intelligence
Panelists:
Jason Daniels, Sales Manager, Tongwei Co., Ltd.
Pengcheng Kang, GM of Europe Region, Svolt Energy Technology Co., Ltd.
Gonzalo Muley, BESS Business Development Manager, LONGi Europe
Michael Alexander Strobel, Director of European Business, Great Power
Keynote Speech: How Battery Innovation Can Enable the Next Energy Era
Speaker: Laura Azpilicueta, EMEA Business Development Director, Ampace
Panel Discussion: How Next-Generation Module Technologies (TOPCon, HJT, BC, CPV) Reshape Project Profitability in Europe
Moderator: Uriel Wang, Senior Analyst for PV and Power Market, SMM
Panelists:
Laurent Bodin, Chief Commercial Officer, Holosolis
Dr. Frank Dimroth, Head of III-V Photovoltaics and Concentrator Technology, Fraunhofer ISE/Clearsun Energy
Edgardo Lagos, Regional Manager Spain, SUNTEC
Laura Azpilicueta, EMEA Business Development Director EMEA, Ampace
The panelists noted that modules manufactured locally in Europe can provide value in terms of supply chain balance, local job creation, and quality control, so a moderate price premium is justified. TOPCon is expected to remain the mainstream technology in the European market over the next 2–3 years; back-contact (BC) and tandem technologies are under evaluation for longer-term deployment. On cross-regional cooperation, the European and Chinese industries should maintain open collaboration and avoid trade barriers to jointly advance the global energy transition.
Keynote Speech: How Concentrator Photovoltaic (CPV) Technology Will Shape the Future of Solar Energy Conversion
Speaker: Frank Dimroth, Head of III-V Photovoltaics and Concentrator Technology, Fraunhofer ISE/Clearsun Energy
Keynote Speech: Getting to Know Sigenergy: Smart Solar and Storage from Home to Utility Plant
Speaker: Óscar Pereiro, Solutions and Services Manager Spain, Sigenergy
November 3: Keynote Speech
Keynote Speech: Designing Hybrid Systems to Create Long-Term Value
Speaker: David Cruañes Lee, Iberia Technical Director, TBEA Xi'an Electric Technology Co., Ltd.
Panel Discussion: A Key Pillar of European Energy Transition: Unlocking the Growth Potential of Distributed Solar-Storage
Moderator: Roman Schilin, Investment Manager, Encavis
Panelists:
Nicolas Daunis, General Manager, Green Yellow Spain
Carlota Pi, Co-founder and CEO, Holaluz
Rafael Hernández, Head of Business Development / M&A Director, ReENE EU ENERGY
The panelists noted that, from the perspective of independent power producers (IPPs), large-scale PV+ESS integration (PV+BESS) projects are the core means of avoiding losses from negative electricity prices and boosting returns (by up to 40%), while grid connection access conditions are the most valuable asset for new projects. The motivations of different players vary. Industrial users seek "behind-the-meter self-protection" to hedge against electricity price fluctuations, improve power quality, and mitigate grid risks, while residential users are transformed from "passive consumers" into "dispatchable resources" through VPPs. The former prioritizes stability, while the latter seeks returns, so products and business models cannot be treated as one-size-fits-all. The real bottleneck lies in the mechanisms. Spain's transmission network is already 83% saturated; residential batteries can be installed within days, but large projects face waits of 2–3 years. It is therefore recommended to draw on Australia's example by introducing independent aggregators and providing subsidies or low-cost financing for distributed energy storage.

evidence.title: Ola Electric’s Q2 loss narrows despite a fall in revenue, deliveries
evidence.text:
EV maker Ola Electric narrowed its losses even as revenues and deliveries declined in the second quarter of FY27. Its net loss narrowed 13 per cent year-on-year (y-o-y) to ₹362 crore, down from ₹418 crore in the same quarter last year. However, revenue declined 39 per cent to ₹421 crore.
Deliveries fell to 34,667 vehicles in the second quarter, from 52,666 vehicles in the year-ago period.
Operating expenses stood at ₹369 crore, down from ₹390 crore in the first quarter, excluding a one-time non-cash reversal of ₹57 crore recorded in Q1.
The company is shifting to a dealer-led distribution model, having shut down most of its company-operated stores. Its first dealer stores went live on September 4. By November 8, the network had expanded to 255 dealer partners operating 319 stores. Ola Electric plans to increase this to around 450 stores by December and 700 by March 2027. All new production is now being routed through dealers.
The company said production, which had remained broadly flat for several months, is now increasing month on month. It expects to produce around 25,000 vehicles in December.
“Wholesales are ramping, and dealers are reordering, which has strengthened the flywheel. Demand is not our constraint; the constraint is the ramp-up of our supply chain,” the company said.
During the quarter, Ola Electric also raised funds through a qualified institutional placement (QIP). Its total borrowings declined from ₹3,132 crore in December 2024 to ₹1,819 crore in September 2026. Auto borrowings, specifically, fell from ₹2,422 crore to ₹337 crore over the same period.
The company added that it expects its battery requirements to comprise around 30 per cent nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) cells and 70 per cent lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells. The focus remains on meeting its own automotive requirements. Ola noted that its NMC cell yields currently stood at 70-75 per cent and were expected to improve to 80-85 per cent by the end of Q3 FY27 and around 90 per cent in Q4 FY27.
With the growth in its automotive business, Ola Electric expects the segment to consume around 2-3 GWh of battery capacity in FY28.

evidence.title: Ola Electric’s Dealer Network Shift Tests India’s EV Supply Chain
evidence.text:
Ola Electric’s September-quarter results point to a deeper transition in India’s electric two-wheeler market than a narrower quarterly loss might suggest. The company is replacing much of its direct-to-consumer retail network with dealers, cutting borrowings and trying to increase production, while acknowledging that supply—not demand—is now the main constraint on its automotive business.
The company reported a consolidated net loss of Rs 362 crore for the September quarter, narrower than the Rs 418 crore loss recorded in the corresponding quarter last year. That improvement, however, came alongside a steep fall in revenue from operations, which declined 39% year-on-year to Rs 421 crore from Rs 690 crore. Sequentially, the loss widened from Rs 336 crore in the June quarter and revenue fell 7.5% from Rs 455 crore.
These figures show why Ola’s immediate challenge is not simply profitability. The company is attempting to redesign the way it reaches customers, finances inventory and scales vehicle production at the same time. That makes the result relevant to the wider urban mobility system, where electric two-wheelers depend not only on vehicle technology but also on retail access, after-sales support, charging availability and reliable delivery networks.
The most consequential change is the move away from Ola’s direct-to-consumer model. In its shareholder letter, the company said it had appointed 255 dealer partners operating 319 stores as of November 8, 2026. It plans to expand that network to 450 stores by December and 700 stores by March 2027. Ola stopped accepting orders through its direct-to-consumer stores on November 1 and expects to close most of those outlets by December.
The transition changes the financial responsibilities within the sales chain. Under the new dealer model, dealers pay for vehicles when placing orders and hold inventory at their stores. Ola said this would reduce its working-capital requirements and lower operating expenses by another Rs 50 crore as company-operated stores are shut. In effect, the company is seeking to move some of the cost and inventory burden away from its own balance sheet while expanding physical market coverage through partners.
That model may improve the company’s cash position, but it also makes execution dependent on the quality and reach of the dealer network. A company-operated outlet gives the manufacturer direct control over sales, inventory and customer interaction. A dealer-led network requires coordination across independent businesses, including order placement, vehicle availability, service and local market coverage. The supplied results do not establish how individual dealers will perform, but they make clear that distribution has become a central operating variable for Ola.
The company’s financial position has improved in one important respect. Total borrowings declined to Rs 1,819 crore in September 2026 from Rs 3,132 crore in December 2024, while borrowings in the automotive business fell to Rs 337 crore from Rs 2,422 crore over the same period. Ola attributed the reduction to its qualified institutional placement and rights issue. It expects the automotive business to generate positive free cash flow in the near term, supported by lower debt, reduced operating expenses and an improving working-capital cycle.
The figures also show that lower debt has not yet solved the operating problem. Free cash flow remained negative at Rs 371 crore in the September quarter, compared with negative Rs 351 crore in June. Adjusted operating EBITDA loss stood at Rs 246 crore, narrower than the Rs 258 crore loss a year earlier but wider than the Rs 195 crore loss in the preceding quarter. The adjusted operating EBITDA margin deteriorated to negative 58.5% from negative 42.8% in the preceding quarter.
Gross margin was 29.93% in the September quarter, compared with 30.9% a year earlier and 30.5% in June. Ola said gross margins could decline slightly during the second half of FY27 because of the transition. That warning is important because the dealer shift is being presented as a route to lower operating costs, but it does not automatically guarantee stronger margins. The company’s cost structure will depend on production volumes, vehicle pricing, dealer economics, inventory movement and the pace at which company-operated stores are closed.
The automotive segment reflects the same tension between scale and financial performance. Revenue declined to Rs 420 crore from Rs 688 crore a year earlier, while the segment’s net loss narrowed to Rs 214 crore from Rs 233 crore. The narrower segment loss alongside lower revenue indicates that cost reduction is already part of the company’s response, but the negative operating cash flow and widening sequential EBITDA loss show that the adjustment remains incomplete.
Ola’s production numbers provide the clearest evidence of the supply-side constraint it described. The company produced 9,235 vehicles in August, 12,284 in September and 14,092 in October. It is targeting production of 20,000 vehicles in November and expects to manufacture 25,000 vehicles in December. Ola said production had started increasing after remaining broadly flat for several months.
The company also disclosed that deliveries of 5,000 vehicles with paid orders were delayed from September to October because of charger unavailability. That detail connects the quarterly results to a practical issue in the EV market: a vehicle sale is not complete from the customer’s perspective if the associated charging equipment is unavailable. The delay also illustrates how a supply chain can constrain deliveries even when demand and manufacturing capacity are not the only limiting factors.
Ola’s statement that “demand is no longer our constraint; supply is” places the company’s current strategy in a different context. The immediate question is not merely whether electric two-wheelers can attract buyers. It is whether manufacturers can synchronise vehicle production, component availability, chargers, retail inventory and service support closely enough to convert paid orders into timely deliveries.
That coordination is particularly important in Indian cities, where two-wheelers form a practical part of daily mobility and where electric vehicles are often adopted for their running-cost advantages. The supplied material does not provide city-level sales, fleet-use or charging data, so it cannot establish how Ola’s transition is affecting specific urban markets. It does show, however, that the consumer-facing EV system extends well beyond the vehicle factory. A dealer store, a charger, a production line and a working-capital decision can all affect whether an urban customer receives and uses an electric scooter.
Ola is also continuing to develop its battery cell manufacturing business. The company said it had achieved the scheduled commercial operation date for 6 gigawatt-hours of manufacturing capacity and that the government had extended the Advanced Chemistry Cell Production Linked Incentive scheme timeline to calendar year 2031. The cell operation gives the company a second industrial focus beyond vehicle assembly, although the results supplied do not establish the capacity’s current output, utilisation or contribution to vehicle costs.
This manufacturing ambition adds another layer to the business transition. Ola is simultaneously reducing retail ownership, lowering automotive borrowings, expanding dealer coverage, increasing vehicle production and developing battery cell capacity. Each step addresses a different constraint: cash tied up in stores and inventory, financing costs, product availability and the long-term supply of a critical EV component. The strategy is therefore not a single turnaround measure but a reorganisation of the company’s operating model.
The policy environment matters because battery manufacturing is linked to the government’s ACC PLI scheme, while the company’s retail and production changes are being driven by commercial pressures. The supplied results identify the scheme extension but do not provide the value of incentives received, eligibility conditions or implementation milestones beyond the revised timeline. Those details would be necessary to assess how much public support contributes to the cell business.
The same limitation applies to the company’s expected improvement in free cash flow. Ola has identified lower debt, reduced operating expenses and a better working-capital cycle as the drivers of near-term improvement. It has also set specific dealer and production targets. But the September-quarter figures show that free cash flow remained negative and that sequential operating losses widened. The evidence therefore supports a conclusion that the transition is under way, not that it has already delivered a completed turnaround.
The larger urban question is whether India’s electric mobility expansion can be supported by operating networks as dependable as the vehicles themselves. Manufacturing scale attracts attention because it is easy to measure in units and gigawatt-hours. Customer experience depends on less visible systems: order fulfilment, charger availability, dealer density, inventory financing and service access. Ola’s results bring those systems into the centre of the EV conversation.
For now, the company’s evidence presents a mixed picture. Borrowings have fallen sharply, the automotive loss has narrowed year-on-year and production is rising from its August level. At the same time, revenue has declined, free cash flow remains negative, the sequential EBITDA loss has widened and paid-order deliveries were delayed by charger shortages. The next meaningful indicators will be whether Ola reaches its planned 450- and 700-store milestones, whether production approaches its November and December targets, and whether the dealer-led model improves cash generation without weakening customer fulfilment.

evidence.title: Ola share price tumbles 6%; Goldman Sachs, Citi, Kotak targets suggest up to 50% downside
evidence.text:
Ola Electric Mobility Ltd shares fell 6 per cent in Friday's trade as at least three brokerages covering the stock maintained 'Sell' ratings on the electric vehicle (EV) maker following its September quarter results. The lowest target price on Ola Electric is from Kotak Institutional Equities at Rs 18 per share, down from Rs 19.64 earlier. Goldman Sachs has a 'Sell' rating with a reduced target of Rs 22 from Rs 23 earlier. Citi has a target of Rs 21, down from Rs 25.07 earlier. The targets suggest up to 50 per cent potential downside from Thursday's closing price of Rs 35.74.
On Friday, the scrip opened 3.37 per cent lower at Rs 34.56 apiece before falling 6.24 per cent to hit a low of Rs 33.50.
The brokerage targets come as Ola Electric Mobility Ltd reported a sequential widening of net losses and a year-on-year (YoY) fall in revenue from operations. The company's consolidated net loss widened to Rs 362 crore in Q2 from Rs 336 crore in Q1 FY27. Ola reported a loss of Rs 418 crore in the year-ago quarter.
"Ola Electric's Q2 Ebitda loss came in higher than our expectations, due to lower volumes and gross margins. Sustenance of volume recovery needs to be seen as brand equity remains weak, in our view. We believe the company will have to work on multiple levers to remain competitive in order to improve its positioning. Ola Shakti is yet to scale up and we will await execution before ascribing any value to this business. FCF outflows pose another challenge and the company risks exhausting its cash reserves if the current volume trajectory does not improve," Kotak said.
Revenue from operations declined 38.99 per cent YoY to Rs 421 crore in the September quarter, compared with Rs 690 crore in the year-ago period.
Operating Ebitda loss stood at Rs 218 crore, against a loss of Rs 203 crore in the corresponding quarter last year.
Separately, addressing shareholders, Ola Electric said, "The QIP and rights issue strengthened our balance sheet, and we have deleveraged significantly. Total borrowings came down from Rs 3,132 crore in December 2024 to Rs 1,819 crore in September 2026."
The company added, "Specifically, Auto borrowings reduced from Rs 2,422 crore to Rs 337 crore. With low Auto debt, a healthy gross margin and cost structure, and a much-improved working capital cycle under the dealer model, we expect Auto to generate free cash flow in the near term."
Commenting on its cell business and growth prospects, the pure-play EV firm said, "The cell macro is also strong, with government focus on components and lithium refining, and growing storage deployments with higher localisation requirements. Through this transformation, our balance sheet is much more stable, our cost base is structurally and meaningfully lower, we are not demand constrained, and we have two long-term growth engines: Auto and Cell."

evidence.title: Ola Electric Q2 results: Net loss narrows to Rs 362 crore, revenue falls 39%
evidence.text:
Ola Electric’s net loss narrowed to Rs 362 crore in Q2FY27, compared with Rs 418 crore reported in Q2FY26.On a quarter-on-quarter basis, the company widened its net loss from Rs 336 crore reported in Q1FY27.
The rise in losses was driven by a sharp reduction in revenue from the company’s core automotive segment.
Ola’s revenue also declined in Q2FY27, falling 39% year-on-year (YoY) to Rs 421 crore from Rs 690 crore reported in Q2FY26. On a sequential basis, revenue declined 7.4% from Rs 455 crore reported in Q1FY27.
Its consolidated operating expenses fell 22% YoY to Rs 369 crore, while EBITDA loss for the quarter stood at Rs 218 crore, rising 7% YoY from EBITDA loss of Rs 203 crore in the same quarter last year.
Ola automotive revenue falls 39%
In the automotive segment, Ola Electric’s revenue fell 39% YoY to Rs 420 crore in Q2 FY27 against Rs 688 crore in the same quarter last year. However, net loss in this vertical contracted to Rs 214 crore from Rs 233 crore in Q2 FY26. Operating EBITDA losses for Q2 FY27 in the automotive segment expanded sharply to Rs 145 crore compared to an EBITDA loss of Rs 102 crore in the year-ago period.
“The main headline of Q2 FY27 is that demand is no longer our constraint; supply is. The constraint is not our manufacturing capacity but our supply chain’s ramp-up, which we are scaling rapidly,” the company said in its shareholder letter.
Ola Electric Mobility share price
On November 12, the stock of Ola ended on the NSE at Rs 35.74, up nearly 4% from its previous close. Over the past one month, its share price has increase by more than 3%, while over the past six months, its stock has declined 1.6%.

Ola Electric Mobility is an Indian electric vehicle (EV) manufacturer incorporated in February 2017. The company is engaged in the development and manufacturing of electric vehicles and key EV components, including battery packs, motors and vehicle frames, through its vertically integrated operations. It also undertakes in-house research and development (R&D) and is developing the Ola Gigafactory for cell production. The company sells its products through a direct-to-customer (D2C) distribution network.

evidence.text:
Ola Electric Mobility Limited has released its Q2 FY27 shareholders’ letter, highlighting a shift in constraint from demand to supply chain ramp-up. The company reported a stable gross margin of 29.9% and a significant reduction in total borrowings to ₹1,819 crore. Key updates include strong dealer momentum for the Auto business and progress in the Cell segment, with plans to scale production and integrate LFP cells into upcoming vehicles.
Ola Electric’s Q2 FY27 Performance and Strategy
Ola Electric Mobility Limited has communicated its Q2 FY27 performance to shareholders, emphasizing a strategic reset and rebuilding of its business model. The company has identified supply chain ramp-up, rather than manufacturing capacity, as the primary constraint for growth. Despite higher commodity costs, the gross margin remained stable at approximately 29.9%. Operating expenses saw a reduction, and the balance sheet has been strengthened through a QIP and rights issue, leading to a significant deleveraging. Total borrowings have decreased from ₹3,132 crore in December 2024 to ₹1,819 crore in September 2026.
Automotive Business Momentum
The Auto business is experiencing strong momentum, with 255 dealer partners operating over 300 stores by November 8th. Wholesales are ramping up, and dealers are reordering, indicating a strengthening flywheel effect. The constraint here is also the supply chain’s ramp-up. Automotive borrowings have been substantially reduced to ₹337 crore. The company is introducing the S1Z in Q4 FY27 at a lower price point with an LFP cell and plans to integrate LFP cells into existing products to reduce bill of materials cost. Industry volumes for E2W (Electric Two-Wheeler) grew by 82.7% year-on-year in Q2 FY27, with EV penetration reaching 11.2%.
Cell Business Expansion
In the Cell segment, Ola Electric achieved its 6 GWh cell capacity target ahead of schedule, and production is ramping up. The Government has extended the ACC PLI to CY2031, with incentives expected from the next quarter. The company highlights its unique position as the only Indian company with commercialized cell manufacturing and technology. The Gigafactory is commissioned, with initial focus on meeting automotive requirements, comprising roughly 30% NMC and 70% LFP. The company expects to consume about 2-3 GWh in FY28 for its auto business. NMC yields are projected to reach 80-85% by the end of Q3 FY27 and 90% in Q4 FY27, while LFP production will begin this quarter, targeting 70% yield by the end of Q4 FY27.
Financial Highlights
Key financial metrics for Q2 FY27 show revenue from operations at ₹421 crore and gross margin at ₹126 crore. Operating expenses were ₹369 crore. The company’s financial reports indicate a continued focus on cost reduction and improving operational efficiency across both its Auto and Cell segments. The integration of LFP cells is expected to provide cost savings, breaking even with buying cells from outside at a 70% yield and offering savings of 10-15% at 85% yield.

evidence.title: Demand no longer a constraint: Ola Electric's Bhavish Aggarwal on Q2 earnings call
evidence.text:
Bengaluru, Ola Electric Chairman and Managing Director Bhavish Aggarwal on Thursday said demand is no longer the electric two-wheeler maker's constraint; supply is, as the company scales up its dealer network and brings its Auto business down to minimal debt.
"Demand is ahead of supply, and we can sell every vehicle we produce," Aggarwal said in a letter to shareholders, shared in a post on X.
The bottleneck is not Ola's own plant, which Aggarwal said in his post already has high installed capacity, but its suppliers. About 5,000 vehicles with paid orders in September were delayed by a week into October because chargers were unavailable.
Aggarwal, in the Q2 FY27 earnings call, reiterated that supplier dependencies are being fixed as partners scale up. Ola expects to produce about 25,000 vehicles in December and intends to clear its paid-order backlog quickly.
The company also shared that it has appointed 255 dealer partners operating 319 stores as of November 8, and plans about 450 stores by December and 700 by March 2027. It stopped taking orders at its own stores on November 1, and most will close by December.
PTI reported on September 4 that the first dealer-operated stores had gone live in seven states.
Aggarwal had also posted on X about Ola Electric's first Dealers Day at its factories in October.
Going from no dealer stores to over 300 in barely two months is a fast build-out for a company that launched its first scooter through a fully company-owned retail network five years ago. Aggarwal said dealers have shown very strong enthusiasm and momentum, and they pay for their vehicles when they order. Channel inventory is about 15 days, and under a week in the earliest stores, and market share in markets where dealers opened early is now well above pre-transition levels, the letter said.

evidence.title: Ola Electric Share Price Falls Over 6% After Q2 Results
evidence.text:
Ola Electric Mobility shares fell more than 6% in early trading on Friday after the electric two-wheeler manufacturer reported a sharp decline in revenue for the September 2026 quarter, despite narrowing its losses.
The Bhavish Aggarwal-led company's stock opened 3.5% lower at ₹34.50, ending a two-session winning streak, before slipping to an intraday low of ₹33.48.
Trading activity remained elevated, with over 15 million shares worth ₹55.63 crore changing hands on the National Stock Exchange (NSE) during the opening five minutes.
Ola Electric reported a consolidated net loss of ₹362 crore for the July-September quarter, compared with ₹418 crore in the corresponding period last year.
However, revenue from operations declined nearly 39% to ₹421 crore from ₹690 crore in Q2 FY26.
Total expenses fell approximately 28% to ₹639 crore, against ₹893 crore a year earlier.
The automotive division reported a loss of ₹214 crore, narrowing from ₹233 crore in the previous year's corresponding quarter.
Segment revenue also declined to ₹420 crore from ₹688 crore.
The results reflected lower sales revenue alongside reductions in expenditure across the business.
The company is restructuring its retail network by replacing company-owned outlets with dealer-operated stores.
Ola Electric opened its first dealership on Sept 4 and expanded the network to 319 outlets by Nov 8.
The transition forms part of the company's strategy to reduce operating expenses and improve the efficiency of its distribution operations.
According to the company, operating costs have already declined and are expected to fall by another ₹50 crore as it closes its company-operated store network.
The restructuring comes as Ola Electric seeks to contain losses and streamline operations amid pressure on revenue.
Investors will be watching whether the dealership expansion and cost reductions translate into improved financial performance in subsequent quarters.

evidence.title: Ola Electric Q2 FY27: Losses Deepen Amid Revenue Collapse and Market Share Erosion
evidence.text:
The ₹18,115 crore market capitalisation company's stock closed at ₹35.73 on November 12, 2026, up 3.75% for the day but down 15.99% over the past year, significantly underperforming the Sensex's 3.03% decline and the broader Automobiles sector's 16.51% gain. The quarterly performance reveals a company struggling with fundamental business model challenges as operating losses persist and cash burn continues unabated.
The September 2026 quarter results paint a grim picture of operational distress, with the company burning ₹218.00 crores in operating losses before other income—a margin of negative 51.78%. This represents a significant deterioration from the already concerning negative 36.26% margin in Q1 FY27, indicating that scale is working against the company rather than in its favour. The sequential revenue decline of 7.47% from Q1 FY27's ₹455.00 crores compounds concerns about demand sustainability and competitive positioning.
Quarterly Trend: Consistent Deterioration Across Metrics
Financial Performance: Revenue Collapse Exposes Business Model Fragility
Ola Electric's Q2 FY27 revenue of ₹421.00 crores represents a catastrophic 38.99% year-on-year decline from ₹690.00 crores in Q2 FY26, marking the company's weakest quarterly performance in recent history. The sequential decline of 7.47% from Q1 FY27 further underscores deteriorating market position. On a half-yearly basis, H1 FY27 revenues stood at ₹876.00 crores, down 42.29% from H1 FY26's ₹1,518.00 crores, indicating systematic market share erosion rather than temporary setbacks.
Operating losses before other income widened dramatically to ₹218.00 crores in Q2 FY27 from ₹203.00 crores in Q2 FY26, despite revenues falling by nearly 39%. This inverse relationship between scale and profitability suggests fundamental unit economics challenges. The operating margin excluding other income deteriorated to negative 51.78% from negative 29.42% a year ago—a staggering 2,236 basis points deterioration that reflects pricing pressures, elevated manufacturing costs, and insufficient volume leverage.
The company's gross profit margin collapsed to negative 60.33% in Q2 FY27 from negative 35.65% in Q2 FY26, indicating the company is selling products below direct manufacturing costs. PAT margin deteriorated to negative 85.99% from negative 60.58%, demonstrating that losses are accelerating faster than revenue decline. Interest costs of ₹63.00 crores and depreciation of ₹108.00 crores in Q2 FY27 add significant fixed cost burdens that amplify operational challenges.
Operational Crisis: Negative Returns and Capital Destruction
Ola Electric's operational metrics reveal a company in severe distress. The average return on capital employed (ROCE) stands at negative 45.14%, with the latest reading at negative 36.66%, indicating the company destroys substantial value on every rupee of capital deployed. Return on equity (ROE) averaged 0.0% over the assessment period, with the latest reading at negative 54.70%, demonstrating catastrophic shareholder value destruction.
The company's balance sheet shows shareholder funds of ₹3,351.00 crores as of March 2026, down from ₹5,143.00 crores in March 2025—a decline of ₹1,792.00 crores driven by accumulated losses. Long-term debt stood at ₹1,188.00 crores, down from ₹1,724.00 crores, whilst current liabilities of ₹2,849.00 crores include trade payables of ₹679.00 crores. The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.36 appears manageable, but the company's negative cash generation raises questions about refinancing capability.
Cash flow analysis for FY26 reveals operating cash outflow of ₹775.00 crores, a significant improvement from FY25's ₹2,391.00 crores burn but still deeply negative. The company generated ₹2,002.00 crores from investing activities in FY26—likely from asset sales or investment liquidation—which funded operations and reduced debt. However, this is unsustainable, and the company consumed ₹1,201.00 crores in financing activities, indicating limited access to fresh capital.
Critical Red Flags: Structural Profitability Challenges
Unit Economics Crisis: Negative gross margins of 60.33% indicate the company sells each vehicle below direct manufacturing cost, suggesting fundamental pricing power issues or unsustainable cost structures.
Scale Disadvantage: Operating margins deteriorating despite industry maturation suggests fixed cost burdens and competitive pressures are overwhelming any volume benefits.
Capital Destruction: ROE of negative 54.70% and ROCE of negative 36.66% demonstrate systematic shareholder value destruction with no path to profitability visible.
Cash Burn Trajectory: Despite improved cash flow metrics in FY26, the company still burned ₹775.00 crores operationally, raising sustainability concerns without fresh capital infusion.
Market Context: Losing Ground in Competitive EV Landscape
Ola Electric's struggles occur against a backdrop of intensifying competition in India's electric two-wheeler market. Established players like Hero MotoCorp and emerging competitors like Ather Energy have gained market share whilst Ola's revenues have collapsed. The company's 38.99% year-on-year revenue decline in Q2 FY27 far exceeds any market contraction, indicating specific company-level execution failures rather than sector-wide challenges.
The electric two-wheeler segment has witnessed pricing pressures as subsidy support under the FAME-II scheme phases down, whilst battery costs remain elevated. Ola's inability to pass through costs—evidenced by negative gross margins—suggests weak brand positioning and limited customer loyalty. Quality concerns, service network gaps, and product reliability issues have reportedly driven customers towards competitors with more established after-sales infrastructure.
The company's five-year sales growth of negative 41.06% contrasts sharply with the sector's overall expansion, highlighting systematic market share loss. Whilst the broader Automobiles sector delivered 16.51% returns over the past year, Ola Electric declined 15.99%, underperforming by 32.50 percentage points. This divergence reflects investor recognition that Ola's challenges are company-specific rather than industry-wide.
Peer Comparison: Valuation Premium Without Fundamental Support
Ola Electric trades at a price-to-book value of 5.33x despite being loss-making with zero return on equity. This compares to Hero MotoCorp's 4.57x P/BV backed by 21.55% ROE and consistent profitability. Profitable peers like Escorts Kubota (10.68% ROE) trade at just 2.20x book value, whilst Force Motors (14.82% ROE) commands 5.64x. Ola's valuation premium appears unjustifiable given its negative returns and deteriorating fundamentals.
Direct competitor Ather Energy, also loss-making, trades at a significantly higher 17.79x book value, reflecting either market optimism about its turnaround prospects or irrational valuation. Ola's lower multiple suggests the market has partially priced in execution risks, but at 5.33x book value for a company destroying capital at negative 54.70% ROE, substantial downside risk remains. The company's enterprise value to sales ratio of 10.15x appears excessive for a business with negative margins and declining revenues.
Valuation Analysis: Risky Premium for Capital-Destroying Business
At ₹35.73, Ola Electric trades at 5.33 times book value despite generating zero returns on equity and operating at deeply negative margins. The company's valuation grade stands at "Risky"—a designation reserved for businesses with fundamental profitability concerns. With enterprise value to EBITDA at negative 20.74x (meaningless for loss-making companies) and EV to capital employed at 4.17x, traditional valuation metrics offer little guidance beyond confirming overvaluation.
The stock trades 25.76% below its 52-week high of ₹48.13 but remains 71.53% above its 52-week low of ₹20.83, suggesting significant volatility and uncertainty about intrinsic value. The absence of earnings makes P/E ratio analysis impossible, whilst the lack of dividends eliminates yield-based valuation. The company's negative cash generation and mounting losses suggest fair value substantially below current levels, potentially closer to book value of ₹7.46 per share—implying 79% downside risk.
Shareholding Pattern: Institutional Scepticism Evident
Promoter holding has declined from 36.78% in September 2025 to 32.97% currently, with significant dilution occurring between December 2025 and March 2026 (down 2.19 percentage points) and again between March and June 2026 (down 1.62 percentage points). This systematic reduction suggests either capital raising requirements or promoter confidence concerns. The current 32.97% stake, whilst still substantial, reflects diminished skin in the game.
Foreign institutional investor (FII) holdings remain minimal at 4.73%, up marginally from 4.11% last quarter but still reflecting limited global investor interest. Mutual fund holdings of 8.22% decreased from 8.52% in Q1 FY27, indicating domestic institutional investors are reducing exposure. Combined institutional holdings of just 16.48% underscore widespread scepticism about the company's turnaround prospects. Insurance company holdings of merely 0.02% further confirm institutional wariness.
The dominant 50.55% non-institutional holding creates volatility risk and suggests the stock is largely held by retail investors who may lack the analytical depth to assess fundamental deterioration. With 13.11% of shares pledged, refinancing risks emerge if the stock price continues declining. The shareholding pattern reveals a company struggling to attract or retain sophisticated institutional capital—a significant red flag.
Stock Performance: Severe Underperformance Across All Timeframes
Ola Electric has delivered negative returns of 15.99% over the past year, underperforming the Sensex by 12.96 percentage points. The two-year picture is catastrophic, with the stock down 51.01% whilst the Sensex gained 4.11%—a staggering 55.12 percentage point underperformance. Short-term performance offers no respite, with the stock declining 8.72% over three months versus the Sensex's 5.06% gain, generating negative 13.78 percentage points of alpha.
The stock's beta of 1.35 indicates it is 35% more volatile than the broader market, amplifying both gains and losses. However, with a risk-adjusted return of negative 0.26 and volatility of 61.31%, the stock falls squarely into the "high risk, low return" category—the worst possible combination for investors. The Sharpe ratio is negative, confirming investors are not compensated for the substantial risk undertaken.
Technical indicators paint a mixed picture, with the stock recently turning "mildly bullish" on November 11, 2026, after prolonged sideways and bearish trends. However, trading below all major moving averages (5-day, 20-day, 50-day, 100-day, and 200-day), the stock faces multiple resistance levels. The 52-week low of ₹20.83 provides downside support, but further deterioration in fundamentals could test these levels again.
Investment Thesis: Below Average Quality Meets Risky Valuation
Ola Electric's investment thesis is fundamentally challenged across all parameters. The company carries a "Below Average" quality grade, reflecting weak long-term financial performance characterised by negative sales growth of 41.06% over five years, average ROCE of negative 45.14%, and systematic cash burn. The "Risky" valuation designation underscores that even at current depressed levels, the stock trades at unjustifiable premiums given its capital destruction trajectory.
The company's financial trend is classified as "Negative," with the latest six-month performance showing net losses growing 42.29% year-on-year and quarterly revenues declining 10.40% versus the previous four-quarter average. evidence.title: Reliance, JSW, Exide among 22 bidders for 10 GWh battery PLI scheme
evidence.text:
Reliance Industries, JSW Neo Energy, Exide Energy Solutions and Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies are among 22 companies that have bid for 10 GWh of advanced chemistry cell (ACC) battery manufacturing capacity under the government’s production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme, signalling growing interest among large industrial players in the country’s emerging energy storage market.
The Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) opened technical bids on Wednesday for the capacity, which is earmarked for grid-scale stationary storage applications and forms part of the government’s broader target of establishing 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity.
The list of bidders also includes renewable energy companies such as ACME Solar Holdings, Avaada Electro, Waaree Energy Storage Solutions and Vikram Solar, alongside power equipment manufacturers Fujiyama Power Systems and Shirdi Sai Electricals.
The tender comes more than five years after the scheme was approved by the Union Cabinet in May 2021, with a budgetary outlay of Rs 18,100 crore to incentivise the establishment of 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity. The Centre initially allocated the entire capacity to four companies in March 2022 — Ola Electric (20 GWh), Hyundai Global Motors (20 GWh), Rajesh Exports (5 GWh) and Reliance New Energy Solar (5 GWh).
However, Hyundai Global Motors withdrew from the scheme in August 2022 after Hyundai Motor Company publicly clarified that it had no association with the company and that the latter was not authorised to use its trademark. The withdrawal left 20 GWh unallocated, prompting MHI to initiate fresh bidding rather than distribute the capacity among companies on the original waiting list.
The government subsequently divided the vacant capacity equally between battery manufacturing for mobility applications and grid-scale stationary storage. Reliance Industries secured 10 GWh in a subsequent bidding round, with the programme agreement signed in February 2025. The remaining 10 GWh was reserved for stationary storage, with the allocation process initiated earlier this year.
Under the programme, beneficiary firms are required to establish manufacturing facilities before receiving incentives on the sale of domestically manufactured cells.
However, the pace of commercial production has remained slower than initially envisaged. According to MHI, only 1 GWh of manufacturing capacity had been installed under the scheme as of March 2026, despite 40 GWh having been allocated to beneficiary firms.
The latest tender is expected to complete the allocation process for the programme’s targeted 50 GWh capacity, even as the industry continues to work towards scaling up domestic battery manufacturing.

evidence.title: Exide Redefines Customer Experience with AI and Salesforce
evidence.text:
Exide Redefines Customer Experience with AI and Salesforce
Salesforce today announced that Exide Industries, one of India’s leading battery and energy solutions companies, is leveraging Salesforce to unify customer engagement, laying the foundation for the next generation of customer and service excellence. By unifying data, AI, and operations, Exide is enabling smarter decision-making and delivering seamless, connected experiences across its B2B and B2C businesses.
Exide has deployed Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, Field Service Cloud, Marketing Cloud, and Experience Cloud to bring the full customer lifecycle together on a single platform. Today, Salesforce unifies Exide’s ecosystem of more than 120,000 dealers, 20,000 mechanics, 6,000 service technicians and 1,000 sales personnel nationwide, giving teams a 360-degree view of customer interactions, service histories, warranties, and partner operations across the customer lifecycle. Service response times have reduced from days to hours, while complaint resolution turnaround times have improved by over 30%, helping Exide deliver faster and more effective customer support. More than 95% of complaints are now resolved in a single visit.
Sales Cloud has strengthened opportunity management, pipeline visibility and lead conversion across its B2B and B2C businesses, supporting a more disciplined and data-driven sales process. Service Cloud has helped transform customer engagement from a reactive model to a more connected, proactive experience. More than 80% of customer interactions are now driven through self-service channels, with over 500,000 monthly service tickets managed through WhatsApp-enabled customer journeys integrated with Salesforce workflows. Field Service Cloud powers Exide’s “Batmobile” doorstep assistance service, automatically connecting customers with the nearest field technician for rapid response and on-site support across the top 100 cities in India — often within 30 minutes. The unified platform also enables improved dealer engagement, better sales visibility, faster warranty processing, and richer customer insights across Exide’s nationwide network.
As part of its continued digital transformation journey, Exide’s roadmap includes AI agents supporting sales, customer support, warranty intelligence, multilingual customer conversations, predictive diagnosis, and autonomous service operations. India’s mobility ecosystem is changing rapidly with EVs, connected vehicles, digitized service expectations, and omnichannel customer engagement. Exide is investing in AI-driven customer operations to stay ahead of these changing expectations.
Ravi Kumar, Chief Digital & Information Officer, Exide Industries, said, “Our vision extends beyond digitizing processes. We are building an intelligent customer operations platform where data, AI, and automation work together to anticipate customer needs, empower our dealer ecosystem and enable our teams to make faster decisions. Salesforce provides the digital foundation that supports this vision while helping us continuously elevate customer experience.”
Mankiran Chowhan, Managing Director, Salesforce India, said, “The next era of manufacturing will be driven by industrial intelligence — where connected data, AI-powered insights, and operational systems converge to enable smarter decisions from the factory floor to the boardroom. Exide’s end-to-end transformation demonstrates how organizations can modernize field operations, service delivery, and partner engagement holistically on a single trusted platform. We are proud to partner with Exide as they continue building a more connected, data-driven, and AI-powered customer operations ecosystem.”

evidence.title: RIL, Amara Raja, Exide, among 22 companies to bid for 10 GWh battery storage capacity PLI
evidence.text:
The Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) on Thursday said it has received 22 bids for 10 GWh of advanced chemistry cell (ACC) manufacturing capacity under the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme from companies including Reliance Industries, ACME Solar Holdings, Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies, Exide Energy Solutions, JSW Neo Energy, and Vikram Solar.
The 10 GWh capacity is earmarked for Grid-Scale Stationary Storage (GSSS) applications and forms part of the overall targeted 50 GWh ACC manufacturing capacity under the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage.
“The allocation of 10 GWh for GSSS applications is expected to support the country’s rapidly growing energy-storage requirements arising from the expansion of renewable energy. It will contribute to enhancing energy security and deepening the domestic value chain for ACC technologies,” the MHI said.
In May 2021, the Cabinet approved the scheme, with a total budgetary outlay of ₹18,100 crore. It seeks to enhance the domestic ACC manufacturing capabilities and encourage large domestic and international players to establish a globally competitive ACC manufacturing ecosystem in India, MHI said.
The request for proposal (RFP) was floated on the Central Public Procurement (CPP) portal on July 15, 2026, while the pre-bid conference was held on July 29. The last date for bid submission was November 10, and the technical bids were opened the following day in the presence of bidders at the MHI, it said in a statement.
“The bidding is being conducted online through a transparent two-stage Quality and Cost-Based Selection (QCBS) mechanism,” the Ministry said, adding that the strong participation in the tender reflects growing industry interest in India’s ACC manufacturing potential and reinforces the government’s commitment to building a technologically self-reliant, globally competitive and sustainable ACC ecosystem.
Other bidders include Avaada Electro, Fujiyama Power Systems, Megha Engineering and Infrastructures, Waaree Energy Storage Solutions, Godawari New Energy, Renew Photovoltaics and Sun Drops Energia. The list also carries names such as GK Energy, JPM Energy Solutions, Lineage Power, Mahendra Sponge and Power, Nsure Reliable Power Solutions, Sai Bioenergy, Shirdi Sai Electricals, Utex New Energy, and Zetsol Energy.

Exide Industries Integrates Sales, Service Operations With Salesforce AI Platform
Exide Industries has integrated its sales, service and dealer network on Salesforce, reporting over 30% improvement in complaint resolution turnaround times and more than 95% of complaints resolved in a single visit.
Exide Industries has integrated its sales, service, field operations and dealer network on Salesforce, using the platform to manage customer interactions across its business-to-business (B2B) and business-to-consumer (B2C) operations. The company has reported a reduction in service response times from days to hours and an improvement of over 30% in complaint resolution turnaround times.
The implementation brings together Exide's network of more than 120,000 dealers, 20,000 mechanics, 6,000 service technicians and 1,000 sales personnel across India. The platform provides teams with access to customer interactions, service histories, warranty information and partner operations. According to the company, more than 95% of customer complaints are now resolved in a single visit.
Exide has deployed Salesforce's Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, Field Service Cloud, Marketing Cloud and Experience Cloud to manage different stages of the customer lifecycle.
Salesforce Integration Covers Sales And Customer Service
Sales Cloud is being used to manage sales opportunities, pipeline visibility and lead conversion across Exide's B2B and B2C businesses. Service Cloud supports customer engagement and complaint management, with more than 80% of customer interactions now taking place through self-service channels.
The company manages over 500,000 service tickets every month through WhatsApp-enabled customer journeys integrated with Salesforce workflows. The system also supports dealer engagement, sales tracking, warranty processing and access to customer insights across its distribution network.
Exide's Batmobile Service Uses Field Service Cloud
Exide's doorstep assistance service, branded as Batmobile, operates on Salesforce Field Service Cloud. The system connects customers with the nearest available field technician for on-site assistance across the top 100 cities in India. The company said the service can facilitate technician responses within 30 minutes in many cases.
Exide Plans AI Agents For Customer Operations
Exide's next phase of digital integration includes AI agents for sales, customer support, warranty intelligence and multilingual customer interactions. The roadmap also covers predictive diagnosis and autonomous service operations.
The company said its investments in AI-driven customer operations are intended to address changing service requirements associated with electric vehicles, connected vehicles and digital customer engagement.
Ravi Kumar, chief digital and information officer at Exide Industries, said the company's objective is to develop a customer operations platform that combines data, AI and automation to anticipate customer requirements, support its dealer network and improve decision-making.
The development comes as Exide continues to expand its presence in lithium-ion battery manufacturing through its wholly owned subsidiary, Exide Energy Solutions. The subsidiary is establishing a greenfield lithium-ion cell manufacturing facility in Bengaluru, with an initial planned capacity of 6 GWh, scalable to 12 GWh.
The facility will have four production lines covering cylindrical and prismatic cell formats and will cater to lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) chemistries. Installation, validation, customer sampling and homologation activities are at an advanced stage, with the facility expected to move towards operationalisation during FY27.

evidence.title: Exide beats Amara in Q2, but returns from lithium-ion investments will decide the winner
evidence.text:
Automotive battery makers Exide Industries and Amara Raja Energy & Mobility posted contrasting results for the September quarter (Q2FY27). Exide’s standalone Ebitda rose nearly 54% year-on-year to ₹606 crore as revenue improved 20% to ₹5,026 crore. In contrast, Amara saw Ebitda fall 5% year-on-year to ₹386 crore—hurt by a sharp increase in input costs such as metal alloys and sulphuric acid—even as revenue grew 13% to ₹3,843 crore.
Exide’s Ebitda growth reflects strong market demand and its ability to pass on cost inflation. It hiked prices of four-wheelers by about 10% and two-wheelers by 5% during January-October. Q2FY27 gross margin rose 75 basis points (bps) year-on-year to 30.6%. Other costs dropped by over 170 basis points, though this came on a high base created when consumers deferred purchases ahead of last year’s GST rate cut, resulting in adverse operating leverage. Amara Raja managed only limited price hikes — 2% in Q2 after 3% in Q1 — causing its gross margin to shrink by about 300 basis points to 29.8%.
Betting big on lithium-ion
With the industry transitioning from lead-acid to lithium-ion technology, both companies are investing heavily to keep pace. Exide commenced commercial production at its lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery plant and began recognising revenues in October. Meanwhile, its wholly owned subsidiary, Exide Energy Solutions Ltd (EESL), commissioned a 6 GWh lithium-ion cell facility in Q2. EESL manufactures and supplies advanced-chemistry cells, modules, and battery packs for both electric vehicles (EVs) and stationary energy storage systems.
India’s growing demand for electric two-wheelers (E2Ws) provides scope for growth. Monthly E2W sales have touched about 200,000 units this year, compared with 120,000 units last year, Exide said. So far in FY27, the company has invested ₹5,352 crore in EESL. “With EV inflection, Exide can gain significantly in the medium term if it executes well on Li-ion cell production, though it may take one or two years for yields to stabilise and to achieve the right scale,” said Nomura Global Markets Research.
Amara’s 10GWh battery energy storage solution plant is expected to start commercial production in Q4FY27. It also announced an investment of ₹2,320 crore to set up a 5 GWh LFP battery manufacturing facility and increase the capacity of its Li-ion factory. So far, it has invested ₹2,100 crore in total in the new energy business, which accounts for about 6% of consolidated revenue and encompasses lithium-ion technology, clean energy storage, and electric mobility solutions.
Both battery makers face significant risks due to their heavy capital commitments, as the long-term commercial viability of lithium-ion technology remains unproven. Also, because global lithium-ion cell manufacturing is inherently low-margin, the pivot could dilute returns. For Amara Raja, higher procurement costs for alloys, sulphuric acid and polypropylene, coupled with rising interest expenses from debt-funded investments in its new energy division threaten to weigh on profitability, said Motilal Oswal Financial Services.
While Exide can fund its LFP cell localization partnership with Hyundai-Kia through internal accruals, Motilal Oswal highlights significant hurdles in its lithium-ion cell venture. The brokerage said most domestic passenger vehicle manufacturers already have in-house battery plans or existing tie-ups, limiting Exide’s total addressable market. Also, Exide is not participating in the production linked incentive (PLI) scheme, which could undermine its cost competitiveness against peers that quality for it.
Both stocks have corrected 29% from their respective 52-week highs in August. So far this calendar year, however, Exide is down just 3%, compared with a 22% drop in Amara Raja. The stocks currently trade at 20 times and 17 times their estimated FY27 earnings, respectively, according to Bloomberg data.
